bridge: B01 covered origins and F03 covered limited authority. Use the fictional app description and official platform references.
teaching:
### Identify what the app can access

A mobile operating system gives apps a sandbox and permission mechanisms. A camera or microphone prompt concerns a particular capability; granting it does not make every later use appropriate. Request only what the feature needs and explain the purpose clearly.

### Protect stored and moving data

Use suitable platform storage for credentials and keys. Check backups, logs, notifications and screenshots as possible places private information can appear. TLS protects a network channel, while server access checks still protect account data.

### Inspect app-to-app entry points

Links, exported components and shared files can let other apps supply data. Validate those inputs and the identity or authority required for sensitive actions. A deep link reaching a screen is not proof the caller may perform its operation.

### Account for the release ecosystem

Signing, distribution and updates help identify packages and deliver changes. Their guarantees depend on platform and deployment rules. Rooted or modified devices change some assumptions but do not remove the need for safe server-side design.

State which platform, version and app configuration the exercise describes before making a broader claim.

These platform questions do not replace native code auditing. Native code is code compiled for the device platform; examining its implementation requires the relevant systems and binary-analysis skills as well as the app-level model.
example:
Fictional offline notes app
Required function: write/read local text notes.
Proposed permissions: camera, microphone, contacts, precise location, network.
No feature uses these capabilities.
Decision: request none of them for the stated function.
If a later scan feature is added: request camera only when invoked,
explain purpose and retain a manual-entry path where feasible.
explanation: Permission need follows the feature and platform contract. “We might use it later” is not sufficient justification. A denied optional permission should not break unrelated note reading. Server data access remains separately scoped to the signed-in account.
exercise: Create a capability/purpose table for the app. Add a photo-attachment feature and define when access is requested, what data is retained and what happens after denial. Use the current official platform guide before claiming exact prompt behaviour.
solution: For the stated offline text-note function, camera, microphone, contacts, precise location and network have no supplied purpose, so the capability table rejects each. For optional photo attachment, offer the platform-supported selection interface when the learner chooses Attach photo, explain the attachment purpose, retain only the selected image under the stated local storage/deletion design, and leave note reading/writing available if selection is cancelled or access denied. Android’s official Photo Picker guide describes a selection route without broad library access; exact availability, fallback and APIs depend on platform/library versions. This paper design is not evidence that a built app implements those choices.
challenge: An exported deep link accepts note_id and account_id from another app. Explain the trust boundary and design checks preventing access to another user's note.
challenge_solution: Treat both fields as untrusted input; derive account identity from trusted session/platform state and authorise the target object. App signing and a valid link format do not prove the caller may select an arbitrary account.
